title: King of The Yees by Lauren Yee at Signature Theatre #kingoftheyees #l...
transcript: I'm always impressed when a play is personal but fantastical, and Lauren Yee has created what feels like an opus in her autobiographical story about her dad and the dying Chinatowns that made him. Framed as a play within a play, it opens with Lauren initially looking to understand her father's devout allegiance to the Yee Family Association. Originally established for mutual aid and social welfare after the California Gold Rush, it's now a seemingly obsolescent Chinese fraternity, at least in the eyes of Lauren. In order to understand this space and why its doors won't open for her, Lauren realizes she first needs to understand her father. What ensues is a genre-bending personal odyssey that's as hilarious as it is illuminating and heartbreaking. I've seen a lot of pieces try to parse through the thorniness of Asian-American identity, and I don't know if anyone has done it so effectively as Lauren has with this piece. Her writing is so richly layered and is able to invoke a myriad of different ideas, ultimately crystallizing into a few main pillars of thought, while leaving very few stones unturned. This sprawling approach provides a lot of comedy and satire, and pretty much everyone gets skewered — her father, Lauren herself, Chinese people in general, American theatre audiences, you name it. Even if you're not Asian or Asian-American, part of the beauty of this piece is how it explores what gets lost between familial generations in general, and how we can close those gaps while honoring what they represent. Between the moving and hysterical script and the stellar cast featuring Tony-winner Francis Jue, King of The Yees at Signature is not to be missed.
